While your argument may have some merit, I believe that merit is more semantic in nature and less important than reality, for lack of a better term. The term "social construct" seems to be one of those terms that, while broadly defined, is essentially used by very specific people for very specific purposes. My arguments are thus:

  1. The term social construct is too broadly defined to have any real meaning.

  2. The term social construct is only used by certain people.

  3. The term social construct is only used for certain purposes.

The term social construct is too broadly defined to have any real meaning

To demonstrate its broad definition, here is the top answer from the very first result I got when I did a search for "social construct definition":

To construct is to build something. A social construct is an idea or concept that people have built, and then they organize their actions and thoughts around it.

Race is a social construct this way: We all are made up of flesh and blood, and need to eat, breathe, drink, and breed to survive as individuals and as a species. Race implies that a person's color or culture should rank or differentiate people with regard to needs and rights and entitlements. Once you peel the skin away and forget where we were born, we are literally all the same. All ideas to the otherwise built around skin color and culture are constructs.

Last time I checked, ideas are only created by humans.

Emphasis mine.

https://answers.yahoo.com/question/index;_ylt=A0LEVz2TT95W7sEAEdNXNyoA;_ylu=X3oDMTEyNmJjZWttBGNvbG8DYmYxBHBvcwMxBHZ0aWQDQjE3OTJfMQRzZWMDc2M-?qid=20110413093816AAaXWIy

The crux of my argument is, what isn't a social construct? What word in the dictionary isn't, at some level, a social construct? Is it even possible for human beings to fathom something into existence and have that something not be a social construct? If most everything is a social construct, the idea that race is a social construct loses its importance. As an analogy, if everyone is responsible, no one is responsible.

The term social construct is only used by certain people

I see this same concept in some US laws, where regulators use broad language that can be interpreted to mean one thing or another. The regulators may have good intentions in trying to cover their bases, but ultimately they (or their judicial counterparts) are the ones that interpret whether someone is following the laws. The regulations cover everyone, but only a select group of people is allowed to interpret the regulations. You may get a different response depending on which regulator you talk to and in general, the regulator will interpret the law to allow themselves more flexibility.

This is similar to the term "social construct", where only certain select people seem to ascribe to its importance (certain college professors, their students, your friendly neighborhood social agitators). I'm sure most have good intentions, but I am suspicious whenever one group of people decides something on behalf of everyone else. Especially when, as in this case, the interpretations of the term are fluid and allow for this select group to have social construct mean whatever they want at any given moment.

The term social construct is only used for certain purposes

It seems to me, that the same crowd that pushes the importance of social constructs is the same crowd that agitate against privilege. Specifically white and male. Occasionally cis or ablest or thin. But privilege is one of those concepts that takes many forms. Its comparatively rare to hear people talk about other privileges, such as regional, parental, height differential, beauty, vocal, mental, immune systems, urban/rural, etc.

To wit, I'll give the concept of race as a social construct more consideration when I see it more consistently applied to people other than whites. I just don't think this idea would gain traction in many parts of the world. People are proud of who they are and what they represent, be it the admittedly ill-fitting term "race" or nationality or local sports team or whatever the term gender refers to this week. And yes, people can belong to multiple groups and represent multiple layers at once. And yes, some people think their group or race or nation is the end all be all and others don't give a shit.

Summary

To summarize, I think your argument has some merit. We all bleed the same and the word "race" is (clears throat) problematic in certain contexts. But group identities (including racial ones) exist, whether the term is correct or not or whether people want to believe it or not. I think the idea here is to get along with reality in tow, not pretend the group differences don't exist.
